messages.author: 1df512834d1d72e8
messages.subject: Local maxima/minima over observation locations
parts:
I am trying to fit a simple spatiotemporal model to surface temperature data. Observational data are available at 16 locations at 1 min time intervals. 

This is how I define my spde, projection matrix, and formula:

```
spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = mesh,prior.range = c(0.05,0.01),prior.sigma = c(1,0.01))

A.est = inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=as.matrix(locs[c("lon","lat")]),group = data$time,n.group=n_minutes)

formula <- (logtemp ~ -1 + Intercept + f(field, model = spde, group = field.group,
                control.group = list(model="ar1")))

```
Subsequently, I predict the response variable (logtemp) on a rectangular grid (1 km x 1km) by simply summing up the mean values for random field and intercept for each time step. The predicted response looks alright i.e., values are within expected range and also the time series at observation locations matches the actual values well. 

However, there is almost always a local minima/maxima at the observation locations e.g., image below which looks like an artifact. 

Is this artifact due to the small range value (r ~ 0.21; using latlon coordinates)?  Fuglstad and Beguin (2018) mentioned that as long as the range is greater than max.edge (0.1 for inner boundary, 0.3 for outer boundary in my case), it should be fine.

What else might be going wrong here?

Thanks!

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Local maxima/minima over observation locations
parts:
Hi,

The posterior mean will always tend to the overall spatial average the further from observations you go, and when the correlation range is short relative to the distance between observations, the effect you see is precisely what should be expected when there isn’t a clear spatial trend within the study region. If you instead plot samples from the posterior distribution, you will likely not see this effect, since the posterior variance will be higher away from the observations.  So I don’t think anything is wrong here.

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Local maxima/minima over observation locations
parts:
To model the effect of moving in space directly, you either need a spacetime 3D anisotropic model, or an advection-diffusion model, or something simple like shifting the coordinates for each timepoint (or more generally a space warping). Neither of these are currently implemented, and for the advection-diffusion case, that’s a major project. Some steps were taken many years ago, but it’s nontrivial. For the space warping version, we did work on that around 15 years ago for local rainfall prediction, but that was pre-inla.

Finn

The advection aspects is in one of the Fuglstad et al papers you can find in the reference list at the end.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Local maxima/minima over observation locations
parts:
I think the formulation of non-stationary SPDE using local anisotropy in Fuglstad et al. (2015) would be able to mimic some of the temperature advection effect. 
Since the observation locations in my dataset also have other meteorological variables such as u and v wind components, I think it is theoretically possible to include local anisotropy.

However, the wind field changes with time (I am fitting a spatiotemporal model, currently with 'ar1') and I am even not sure if it's easily doable in R-INLA as such.
